/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.headline: Nitrite-free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.excerpt: Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats. While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand. Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4. Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%. Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.trail: Shoppers are switching from traditional product despite little evidence alternative is safer

/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.headline: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.excerpt: The boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”. Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designer Arm Holdings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future. Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. “Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. “However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.” Scientists are already using AI-driven tools in cancer research and testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools. Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespread humanoid robots within the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area. “With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said.
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.trail: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years

/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.headline: UK men with heart disease at higher risk of developing and dying from cancer
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.excerpt: Millions of men with heart disease have a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer, according to a decades-long study. The biggest drivers behind male cases were smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol, researchers said, with the link most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers. Analysing health data from 22,000 Britons over 25 years, researchers at the University of Aberdeen and Keele University discovered stark gender differences in outcomes of people living with heart disease. About half the participants – 11,000 – had cardiovascular disease (CVD) at the start of the study, or developed it over the next three decades. The lifetime risk of cancer among those with CVD was higher in men (17.3%) compared with women (12.8%), the study found. In those without CVD, cancer risk was 10.2% among men and 8.2% for women. Dr Tiberiu Pana, a specialty registrar in cardiology at NHS Grampian and honorary early career clinical research fellow at the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that cancer incidence and death were higher in people with cardiovascular disease than in those without – a relationship we already knew a bit about. “However, through looking at this large patient group over a very long period of time we were able to examine it more thoroughly.
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.trail: Decade-long study finds stark gender difference in outcomes of people with heart disease

/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.headline: Cancer cases expected to soar worldwide, WHO report finds
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.excerpt: Remarkable scientific progress against cancer has changed very little for millions of patients globally, who face devastating physical, emotional and financial consequences after diagnosis, a new World Health Organization report has warned. One person in five will develop cancer, according to WHO estimates, and the disease will touch 92% of people, either through their own diagnosis or that of a close family member. Dr Andre Ilbawi, team lead for cancer control at the WHO, said: “For years, the story told about cancer has been about scientific progress, new technologies, new treatment, new hope. That story is true, and it deserves to be told, but it’s not the whole story.” This year’s WHO global status report on cancer found “persistent and widening” inequities in access to prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care. There are an estimated 20.6m cases, and 10m deaths, from cancer every year. Figures are projected to rise to nearly 35m cases by 2050. In richer countries, 85% of those diagnosed with breast or childhood cancers will survive at least five years but the figure drops to less than 30% in poorer countries. In low- and lower-middle income countries, between 9% and 54% of the WHO’s top-20 priority cancer drugs are available, compared with between 68% and 94% in high-income countries, the report found. In 23 countries there are no radiation facilities.
/society/2026/oct/06/cancer-rates-rising.trail: The disease will touch 92% of people globally, finds annual review, while ‘persistent’ inequities found to exist in access to prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care

/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.headline: Japan’s defence minister heads to Australia to meet Marles in wake of melon-gate controversy
/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.excerpt: Japan’s defence minister will visit Canberra this week, the highest level engagement with Australia after controversy over Anthony Albanese’s comments about a gift of melons from prime minister Sanae Takaichi. The defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, will meet his counterpart and deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on Tuesday, with discussions focused on Australia’s acquisition of Japan’s Mogami-class frigates and enhanced security cooperation. Koizumi is considered a potential future prime minister of Japan. His father, Junichiro Koizumi, was prime minister from 2001 to 2006. Koizumi’s visit comes after a week in which Albanese defended himself over comments made on the Bush Deep podcast, released last month. He was discussing a pair of Japanese melons presented by Takaichi during a visit to Canberra earlier this year, and, while appearing to make hand gestures in front of his chest, said “she brought two, as you do”. Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.” Facing days of criticism from the opposition and in the media, Albanese has insisted his hand gestures and a comment about melons were misinterpreted and were not innuendo about breasts. The opposition criticised Albanese for putting at risk close relations with one of Australia’s most important partners in Asia.
/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.trail: Discussions to focus on Australia’s acquisition of Mogami-class frigate as Japan plays down Albanese’s podcast comments

/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.headline: Can Japan avoid a Liz Truss-style shock as its PM embarks on a giant spending spree?
/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.excerpt: International investors are asking where Japan’s prime minister will find the ¥370tn (£1.7tn) of extra cash that she wants to invest in 17 industrial sectors by 2040. Such is the scale of spending by Sanae Takaichi’s coalition government that many in her own party fear she is about to blow up the Japanese economy, triggering a Liz Truss-style economic shock. Nerves are also jangling in financial markets, where investors are stunned by the plans of a usually sober Japanese government to rewrite previous budget rules and embark on a wide-ranging and unfunded shopping spree. The roots of Takaichi’s frustration date back to the financial crisis of 1991, when Japan’s property market bubble burst with spectacular effect. Tokyo had become the world’s most expensive place to live following the country’s export boom, but within months of the crash, banks behind much of the lending were bust. Before the turn of the century, a second slump brought more turmoil when some of Tokyo’s largest financial institutions, unable to cope with the hangover of bad debts from the first crash, went under. In the late 1980s, Japan’s government debts were equal to about 60% of national income, or gross domestic product (GDP). By the end of the 1990s, and after much of the financial sector had been bailed out, the debt to GDP ratio was 130%. Since the 2008 global financial shock, the economy has stagnated.
/world/2026/oct/06/sanae-takaichi-protes.trail: Sanae Takaichi’s blueprint to inject £1.7tn and double economic growth leaves many investors fearful

/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.headline: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.excerpt: Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times. This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base. I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines. Weekend roundup UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.trail: In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his supporters

/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.headline: How Trump changed the way US women vote
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.excerpt: A decade ago, Donald Trump’s improbable presidential campaign was rocked – and nearly derailed – by the now-infamous Access Hollywood tape, a 2005 recording in which the real estate developer turned reality TV star boasted about kissing and grabbing women without their consent. “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” he said, a remark he later downplayed as “locker-room talk” before musing that the tape might be fake. (It wasn’t.) In the moment, it felt fatal – the ignoble end of an explosive campaign for the White House. Back then, Americans hadn’t quite grasped Trump’s capacity to shock but not surprise. Within days, the outrage receded, swallowed by two more “October surprises” – WikiLeaks released the hacked emails of Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and then-FBI director James Comey announced the bureau was reviewing new emails related to her private server. That November, voters punished the first woman to be nominated for president by a major party for her emails, among other grievances, real and imagined, and handed the presidency to the man who had boasted that he could “grab em by the pussy”. US women haven’t voted the same since, and next month’s midterm elections offer another test of their tolerance for Trump in the Trump era. Long divided by race and class, Trump’s rise – or perhaps Clinton’s defeat – splintered US women further, along lines of educational achievement and marital status.
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.trail: A decade after his infamous Access Hollywood tape, the gender divide is again shaping a pivotal midterm election

/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.headline: Trump doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterm elections
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.excerpt: Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in a wide-ranging interview with Time magazine. When confronted with questions about the length of the Iran war, the US president blamed the media for reporting his remarks in which he said the conflict was projected to last “four to five weeks”, in March. “ … I think the press fed it to them,” Trump told Time when asked whether Americans misunderstood him. At the end of March, Trump had told Americans he planned to wind down the Iran war over the next “two to three weeks”. In May, Trump insisted that a peace deal with Iran was nearly finalized. The US president said that he could have ended the Iran conflict whenever but chose to extend it “because I wanted to go further”. For more than seven months, Americans have been grappling with higher everyday costs as a result of Trump’s war with Iran – from gas prices surpassing $4 per gallon to stubborn inflation hovering at 3.4%. Economic concerns, fueled by Trump’s conflict, have angered voters, most of whom say they are unhappy with the president’s handling of the economy and his job overall. Just 26% of adults said they approve of the economy under the Republican president, according to an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.trail: President also dismissed low poll ratings as ‘fake numbers’ and deflected responsibility for Iran war in Time interview

/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.headline: Lawmakers call for action on ‘plainly illegal’ taxpayer-funded ads to promote Trump
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.excerpt: The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections. Two congressional Democrats, Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads. Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”. The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government. “President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.” The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable.
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.trail: House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’

/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.headline: ‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.excerpt: Since the start of his second presidency, Donald Trump has often launched outlandish conspiratorial attacks on critics and foes that mock them and label their views as hoaxes, prompting scholars and legal experts to say Trump’s attacks endanger US freedoms, public health and science. Trump’s extensive use of conspiracy theories is the hallmark of an authoritarian leader that has weakened trust in the coming midterm elections, dangerously ignored scientific evidence, and often pushed for prosecutions of his political enemies in ways that seriously erode civil liberties, say critics. Trump’s conspiratorial and authoritarian-style tactics are palpable say critics, in his false claim that the US faces a “crisis of election security” to bolster his radical push for new curbs on voting rights, and his labeling of climate change as a “hoax” despite extensive scientific evidence that it’s a reality. To some scholars, Trump-backed conspiratorial claims have had a damaging impact on all levels of US society and democracy and are emblematic of how authoritarian leaders use conspiracies to justify repression. Steven Levitsky, the Harvard professor of government and the co-author of How Democracies Die, said: “Conspiracies are page one of the repressive playbook,” noting that Mao, Stalin, Putin and other authoritarian leaders have historically launched attacks on enemies by floating conspiracies.
/us-news/2026/oct/05/donald-trump-approv.trail: President’s outlandish and extensive conspiracy theories endanger US freedoms, health and science, experts say

/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.headline: In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.excerpt: In Spain, tens of thousands of people in 50 cities have taken to the streets amid mounting fury over the country’s housing crisis, their feelings made plain on a banner at the burgeoning protest camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol plaza: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, crypto-bros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.” In France, as high school pupils clash with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system, the angry slogans include: “More hours in class than for sleep”, “Fund study, not repression” and “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”. They may stem from different specific grievances, but the two waves of mainly youth-led protest exemplify a growing problem for western European governments: a generation of young people feeling increasingly denied the basic socioeconomic security that, by and large, their parents enjoyed. The trigger in Spain, where rents have risen by 80% in a decade, was – perhaps ironically – the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid after an investment fund increased her rent by 230%. For those spending more than half their income on housing (the monthly rental on a one-bedroom flat can cost an entire median salary), enough was enough.
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.trail: Demonstrations over housing rights and crumbling schools are a sign the younger generation is withdrawing political consent

/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.headline: Euro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fears
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.excerpt: The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc. The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January. Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election. France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed. Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%. “Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB.
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.trail: France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty

/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.headline: ‘We swept a lot under the carpet’: Vichy regime film hits home in France of 2026
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.excerpt: It is the story of how a lowly state administrator unthinkingly becomes a cog in the machine of an authoritarian regime, embracing the bureaucracy and logistics of sending people to their deaths – and it is drawing in audiences to French cinemas. The French film Notre Salut (Our Salvation), with its modern lighting, improvised scenes and anachronistic 1980s Europop soundtrack, is far from the standard historical costume drama about the second world war. But the award-winning film about the daily lives of ordinary people participating in the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis – and ensured the deportation of a quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps – is poised to become a box office hit. The film, which has been given the English-language title A Man of His Time, had a strong cinema opening in France this week, particularly among young audiences, at a time when the country is soul-searching ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Marine Le Pen of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) continues to top the polls for the presidential race despite the political fallout from an investigation by Mediapart alleging that her party leader, Jordan Bardella, published antisemitic comments as a young party member, which he denies.
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.trail: Movie about Nazi-collaborating administration strikes chord during what director calls ‘time of great uncertainty’

/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.headline: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.excerpt: Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday. Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets. Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices. The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban. Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November. Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.trail: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies

/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.headline: Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protests
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.excerpt: As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class. “We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.” “School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June. “The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week.
/world/2026/oct/05/schoolboy-loses-hand-.trail: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations

/business/2026/oct/05/london-to-chicago-.headline: UK air traffic control chaos disrupts flights for hundreds of thousands of passengers
/business/2026/oct/05/london-to-chicago-.excerpt: Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue into Wednesday at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. At least 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday to and from UK airports had been cancelled, plane tracking site Flightradar24 said, “nearly all at London Heathrow”. More than 1,000 were cancelled by about 8pm on Tuesday. The “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused Britain’s third major stoppage in just over three years. Nats said on Tuesday evening: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. By the time Nats said it had fixed its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart were yet to take off. The disruption spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England. Cancellations and delays continued through Tuesday evening, and British Airways said disruption would affect operations into Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday. Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled.
/business/2026/oct/05/london-to-chicago-.trail: More than 1,000 flights cancelled with problems continuing on Wednesday and airlines calling for overhaul after third incident in just over three years

/uk-news/2026/oct/06/rare-footage-first-.headline: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
/uk-news/2026/oct/06/rare-footage-first-.excerpt: It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese. But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way. The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee. Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything. “You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.” The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow. Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges.
/uk-news/2026/oct/06/rare-footage-first-.trail: Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for the shrill carder bee
